title: Beshalach: bitter water made sweet (Exodus 15:22–26)
hook: at Marah the water is bitter until a tree is thrown in

segments.voice: Yesterday, still in Beshalach, God said go forward at the sea, and the rabbis told of Nachshon stepping in first. Your line was pray, then go forward. Today, three days past the sea, and thirsty.

Big wins have a strange aftertaste. The wedding ends and the thank-you notes begin. The new job starts and the commute is awful. The Israelites have just walked through the sea on dry land and sung a song that is still part of Jewish morning prayer. Three days later, in the wilderness of Shur, they still haven't found water. When they finally do, at a place called Marah, they lift it to their lips and spit it out.
screen: `THE WIN, THEN THE AFTERTASTE.` → `THREE DAYS, NO WATER.` → `MARAH: THEY SPIT IT OUT.`

segments.voice: Marah means bitter. The place is named for its water, and the people do what thirsty people do: they complain to Moses. What shall we drink? Moses cries out to God, and God shows him a tree, a piece of wood. Moses throws it in, and in the old Jewish translation, "the waters were made sweet." A few verses, that's all. The Torah doesn't say what kind of tree it was, and the rabbis couldn't resist asking. In the Mekhilta, an early commentary, several sages each name a different tree. One opinion says it was itself bitter: God can heal bitter with bitter. Another says the tree stands for the words of Torah, which the rabbis link to the tree of life in the book of Proverbs. Then the story ends with a line about God: "for I am the LORD that healeth thee." Notice what the story doesn't do. It doesn't scold them for being thirsty, or take them back to the sea. The bitterness is real; something is thrown into the middle of it, and it changes. Sometimes the change is a tree in the water: a meal someone brings, a joke at the right moment, an old song, a page of something wise. Small things, dropped into the bitter part.
screen: `MARAH: BITTER.` · `A TREE THROWN IN, MADE SWEET.` · `WHICH TREE? THE SAGES DISAGREE.` · `THE LORD THAT HEALETH THEE.` · then, large: `A TREE IN THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Taste one bitter thing honestly, not the biggest, a smaller one: a tense email thread, a chore you hate, a sour mood between you and someone. Ask what small thing could be thrown into it, a kind word, a cup of tea, a walk, a song, and picture dropping it in. If you pray, you can hold the line from Marah: the LORD that healeth thee.
Beshalach. When he let go. Our portion, where just past the sea the water turns bitter, and a tree thrown in makes it sweet.
Your line: a tree in the water. The bitter part can change. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Song at the Sea, sung just before the Marah story, is part of the daily morning service, and the words of Exodus 15:26 about the LORD who heals are echoed in Jewish prayers for healing.

chat.says: So what made the bitter water at Marah turn sweet?
options: Moses threw in a tree God showed him, and the water was made sweet.
The people waited three days, and the bitterness wore off by itself.
Moses struck a rock with his staff, and fresh water poured out.
chat.meaning: God showed Moses a tree; he threw it in and the waters were made sweet. The story ends: I am the LORD that healeth thee.

Marah.meaning: bitter; the place named for its bitter water

Shur.meaning: the wilderness where the people went three days without water

Mekhilta.meaning: an early rabbinic commentary on Exodus

sources.quoted: for I am the LORD that healeth thee.

notes: Exodus 15:25 and 15:26 phrases quoted from JPS 1917 from memory (KJV has the same words); verify.

Mekhilta (Vayassa 1): sages name different trees (willow, olive, oleander/hardufni etc.); one opinion that the bitter tree healed bitter water; and a reading of 'tree' as words of Torah. Confirm the section and opinions.
'A song that Jews still sing every morning': the Song at the Sea (Az Yashir) in Pesukei de-Zimra; confirm.
